title: Aaron Rodgers’ strange NFL trip may be over. The incendiary final act is a fitting last chapter | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

AsAaron Rodgerstore into his head coach on live television, his headphone mic incessantly brushing up against his sweatshirt, he appeared to be a man at peace with ending a glitteringNFLcareer.

Rodgers was once the golden boy in Green Bay, a four-time MVP and Super Bowl champion. He dated movie stars, made the“Discount Double Check”a meme in State Farm ads, and was known as one of the most charismatic off-the-field characters in the league.

He appears set to leave the stage as one of the most baffling personalities in recent NFL history,torching Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy on “The Pat McAfee Show,”the same platform where he became known forCovid-19 skepticism, anti-vaccination takes, political rants and general grumpiness that made those halcyon days in Wisconsin feel very far in the past.

From the moment the Steelers revealed Rodgers would bebenched for Friday’s gameagainst the Denver Broncos, the NFL world readied itself for the quarterback’s response. In fact, most everyone expected him to pop up on McAfee’s show, a place where he regularly appeared before his penchant for getting off hot takes became the worst thing in football: a “distraction.”

But no one quite expected the level Rodgers was ready to go to when he finally popped up on air. Within about two minutes, he had accused McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings, skipping other meetings, not watching game film, questioning his health and alleging that his coach had mistakenly referred to the Steelers as the Packers when breaking a huddle at halftime.

“Last Wednesday, we were in a quarterback meeting. Mike came in late, sat down and within 10 minutes began snoring,” Rodgers said.

“Woke himself up, was rattling his papers, we all looked around. Five minutes later, you hear the snoring again and less than five minutes after that he walks out the room like nothing happened.”

Rodgers said the head coach was then absent from an offensive meeting on Thursday before failing to show at a walkthrough on Friday and missing a morning meeting on Saturday before the Steelers’ game in Philadelphia.

It was during Sunday’s game against the Eagles that Rodgers said McCarthy lost a lot of the team.

“I think the nail in the coffin for so many of us was at halftime, towards the end of it … there’s some rambling or something and without even a heads- up he says, ‘Alright, 1, 2, 3, Packers,’” Rodgers said. “That’s what he broke it down on in the locker room.”

In the lengthy interview, which was mostly a Rodgers monologue broken up by McAfee trying to wrap his head around what he was hearing, the quarterback also accused McCarthy of not taking game planning seriously, not watching enough film, not being as all-in as other high-level NFL head coaches and not really speaking with anyone on the defensive side of the ball.

Complaints about how he was treated were expected. Pulling back the curtain on the Steelers’ 2026 season and setting fire to McCarthy’s reputation? Certainly not.

In a way, the last five years of Rodgers’ career all built to this moment. There is a through line from the moment that he told the media in 2021 thathe was “immunized” against Covid-19– a time when vaccinations were mandatory to play – to his appearance on McAfee on Wednesday.

There was the revelation thathe was taking ayahuascaas part of his off-season preparations, an admission of drug use that likely wouldn’t fly for just about anyone else. Hisdarkness retreat in 2023, when he was considering whether to retire. Therepeated public criticisms of teammatesin Green Bay and New York after he moved to the Jets. A feud with Jimmy Kimmel thatended with Rodgers insinuating a non-existent link between the comedian and Jeffrey Epstein. The flirtation withretiring from football to serve as Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s running mate. And, of course, hison-field remonstrationstoward McCarthy this year.

His prodigious talent allowed him to get away with a lot that teams would not have put up with if he had a lesser résumé. And, when he was benched in Pittsburgh, Rodgers became – in his own words – someone “with nothing to lose.”

And, as he did so often on the field, Rodgers aired it all out. But this time, it’s different.

Rodgers is no longer that time-defying MVP who is carrying his team to victories. He’s much more limited on the field ever since his 2023 Achilles injury. He’s clearly regressed from last season’s AFC North-winning campaign for the Steelers. Part of that isn’t his fault; he’s spent a lot of time on the turf as a leaky offensive line allows pass rushers in.

There are a few possible landing spots for the last few months of Rodgers’ career, which he has said will be over after this season. The New England Patriots are in the hunt andDrake Maye is out for the seasonwith a broken ankle. The Baltimore Ravens and Indianapolis Colts are also facing QB troubles, even though they are largely out of the playoff race.

Even if any of those teams wanted to bring in a new signal-caller to try and improve their offense for the last two months of the regular season, the real question is this: Does anyone want to deal with a guy who just tore apart his last coach?

Quarterbacks are looked at as theultimate leaders in American sports. They are the faces of their franchises, the person everyone on the roster looks to for inspiration in big moments. It’s an outsized job, a level of pressure that is unmatched in the rest of major American sports. A football team needs to have absolute faith in its quarterback in order to be successful.

And maybe that’s what Rodgers thought he was doing. Maybe, in tossing a Molotov cocktail into McCarthy’s already-shaky reputation, he thought he was doing one last solid for the Steelers on the way out the door.

It does seem that something is amiss in Pittsburgh. Local reporters were quick to confirm strife behind the scenes in the Steel City and parts of Rodgers’ tirade were immediately corroborated by unnamed team sources – including the damning allegation of McCarthy falling asleep in a meeting. McCarthy himself didn’t exactly launch a vigorous self-defense in his postgame press conference, declining to discuss private conversations (though he did appear to confirm that he said “Packers” instead of Steelers on Sunday).

He also seemed to confirm the reason why Rodgers was benched in the first place. The quarterback told McAfee that he had met with McCarthy and detailed his problems with the coach before Rodgers demanded the head coach either give up playcalling duties or cut him. McCarthy made clear on Wednesday that the decision was his.

The Pittsburgh coach is about to lead his 11th game as the man in charge of his hometown team. He now faces the task of proving Rodgers wrong about his work ethic, his health, his knowledge of the game and his preparation for each week.

McCarthy won a Super Bowl with Rodgers in Green Bay and together they had many successful years, but he couldn’t get back to that mountaintop – either with Rodgers in Green Bay or without him during his years in Dallas. Now, he’s got Mason Rudolph under center as he tries to salvage a season that seems to have just had the bottom fall out.

If the Steelers do fall apart and McCarthy’s reputation flounders further, it’s possible Rodgers will be proven right. But at what cost?

In January 2023, Rodgers’ Packers were defeated on “Sunday Night Football” by the Detroit Lions, ruining their playoff hopes in the final game of the regular season. Lions safety Kerby Joseph picked him off on his final pass and Rodgers left Lambeau Field for the last time, hanging his head.

He had just turned 39. His successor, Jordan Love, was waiting in the wings. The Packers appeared ready to turn the page and so did he. If that was the moment Rodgers chose to hang up his cleats, he would have left the league a legend who retired near the top of his game, still making incredible throws with his cannon of a right arm.

He would have gone down as a successful quarterback who would always be more known for what he did on the field instead of the controversies he embraced in the last couple of years of his career.

Instead, he appears set to exit the stage as a human torch, setting fire to a season that was in the throes of a playoff push and leaving his former teammates to pick up the pieces.

It’s now possible that the final image of Rodgers as an active NFL player won’t be in uniform,tossing a late-game touchdown on Sundaywith a signature bit of scrambling and deft touch.

Instead, it will be of him on a webcam, unburdening himself to a baffled Pat McAfee and a stoic AJ Hawk. It seems, sadly, a fitting ending.
